title: Government Assistance - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Learn how grants, subsidies, and other Government Assistance reduce your qualified R&ED expenditures in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: In Canada, government assistance for SR&ED includes federal grants such as NRC IRAP and provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. Under the Income Tax Act, it reduces a claimant's section 37 deduction pool and section 127 qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar, although bona fide excluded loans from public authorities are not treated as government assistance.

body.text: In Canada, government assistance for SR&ED includes federal grants such as NRC IRAP and provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. Under the Income Tax Act, it reduces a claimant's section 37 deduction pool and section 127 qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar, although bona fide excluded loans from public authorities are not treated as government assistance.

This report provides a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of the research and development (R&D) tax incentives, direct funding programs, administrative procedures, provincial and territorial regimes, and judicial precedents of Canada as of November 2026.

Canada's flagship federal innovation incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—underwent its most significant legislative expansion in over a decade through the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million, increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Concurrently, Parliament expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out calculation for CCPCs, and extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable credit for the first time to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).

In addition to rate and threshold expansions, the 2024–2026 legislative cycle reversed the 2014 repeal of capital expenditure eligibility by restoring both depreciable capital property and equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 (including First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment [SUE]) to the SR&ED regime. Administratively, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched a voluntary SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval program (Form T1322), providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks that remain valid for up to three years. Meanwhile, at the provincial level, Québec replaced eight legacy innovation tax measures with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (30% on the first $1 million above the exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter) alongside its 2% Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) IP box for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, while British Columbia's Budget 2026 made its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent and aligned its expenditure limit with the federal $6 million cap.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Pillar Statutory Framework under the Income Tax Act and Regulations

The federal SR&ED program is codified within the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX (sections 2900 to 2903) of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Unlike discretionary grant programs, the SR&ED program is an entitlement-based tax incentive embedded in the self-assessment income tax system and administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates tax policy and drafts legislation) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which administers technical and financial compliance, assessments, and refunds).
The statutory architecture operates through two distinct but interconnected tax incentives that must be calculated separately on every claim:

items: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (ITA Section 37): Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to a business of the taxpayer (or a related corporation under subsection 37(1.1)). Rather than being restricted by ordinary capital versus current accounting rules or standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation schedules, expenditures in the subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted in full or in part in the taxation year incurred, or carried forward indefinitely as a running balance to offset business income in any future taxation year.

The SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITA Sections 127 and 127.1): Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), a taxpayer earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a statutory percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of the taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year. The ITC is applied first to reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5). Depending on the claimant's legal status, expenditure type, and expenditure limit, unused ITCs are either refunded in cash as a deemed payment on account of tax under subsections 127.1(1) and 127.1(2) or carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years.

body.text: Crucially, an expenditure may be allowable for the subsection 37(1) deduction pool without qualifying in the same amount—or at all—for the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool, and vice versa. For example, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculated under ITR subsection 2900(4) is a notional overhead amount included exclusively in the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to earn ITCs, but is never added to the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool. Conversely, 100% of an arm's-length Canadian SR&ED subcontractor payment enters the subsection 37(1) deduction pool, whereas only 80% enters the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. Similarly, previously used depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifies for the subsection 37(1) deduction pool but is excluded as a prescribed expenditure under ITR paragraph 2902(b) from earning ITCs under subsection 127(9).
1.2 Mechanics of the Section 37 Pool, Negative Balances, and Loss Restriction Events

The subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures functions as a cumulative multi-year account. Additions that increase the pool balance include current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)), post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)), repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool (paragraph 37(1)(c)), prior-year negative pool income inclusions (paragraph 37(1)(c.1)), pool balances transferred on an amalgamation or wind-up, and prior-year ITC recapture amounts (paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3)).

Conversely, statutory deductions that decrease the subsection 37(1) pool balance include government and non-government assistance (such as provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and federal grants like NRC IRAP) that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing-due date (paragraph 37(1)(d)); provincial super-allowance benefit amounts (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)); federal SR&ED ITCs claimed (applied against tax payable or refunded) in the preceding taxation year (paragraph 37(1)(e)); optional pool deductions claimed by the taxpayer in preceding taxation years (paragraph 37(1)(f)) and insolvency deductions under section 61.3 (paragraph 37(1)(f.1)); and reductions triggered by a loss restriction event under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h).

If deductions from the subsection 37(1) pool—for instance, due to the receipt of government assistance or the paragraph 37(1)(e) reduction from the prior year's federal ITC refund after the taxpayer has already deducted the full Section 37 pool against income—cause the pool balance at the end of a taxation year to become negative, that negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's business income for tax purposes in that year under ITA paragraph 12(1)(v) (or, where applicable to ITCs not reducing the pool, paragraph 12(1)(t)). An equivalent amount is then added back under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) to reset the opening pool balance for the next taxation year to nil ($0).

When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust experiences a change in majority-interest beneficiary), a loss restriction event occurs. A deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately before the acquisition of control, and the undeducted balance of the subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil. Under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h), the pre-acquisition pool is "streamed": it can be reinstated and carried forward to subsequent taxation years only if the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit throughout the subsequent year, and the deduction is restricted to income derived from that same business or a similar business.
1.3 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The legal threshold for all federal and harmonized provincial R&D claims in Canada is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The statute defines SR&ED through an overarching methodological test, three substantive limbs of eligible research, an exhaustive list of eight categories of eligible support work, and seven absolute statutory exclusions.

In its preamble, subsection 248(1) mandates that SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". This core investigation must fall within one of three primary limbs: paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research), defined as "work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view"; paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research), defined as "work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view"; or paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development), defined as "work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto". Experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) is the most commonly claimed category of corporate SR&ED work in Canada.

Once a project satisfies paragraphs (a), (b), or (c), paragraph 248(1)(d) (Support Work) brings into the definition "work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer". Support work does not constitute SR&ED on a standalone basis; it qualifies only when linked directly to a Canadian basic research, applied research, or experimental development project and scaled strictly in proportion (in amount, size, extent, and duration) to the needs of resolving the core scientific or technological uncertainty.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) establish seven absolute statutory exclusions, providing that SR&ED does not include any work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; or (k) routine data collection.

As Canadian jurisprudence and CRA policy emphasize, the exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k) are absolute rather than matters of degree. Where an activity such as data collection or testing is performed, its classification as eligible support work under paragraph (d) versus excluded work under paragraphs (f) or (k) depends on the primary purpose for which the activity was conducted at the time: if carried out specifically to test an SR&ED hypothesis, it qualifies as support work; if carried out for routine business operations or quality assurance, it is excluded even if the resulting data later informs an SR&ED project. Additionally, work carried out inside Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) or airspace is deemed carried on in Canada under ITA subsection 37(1.3).
1.4 Administrative Eligibility Methodology: The "Why" and "How" Framework vs. The Five Questions

Historically, Revenue Canada and the CRA interpreted subsection 248(1) through Information Circular IC 86-4 (1986, revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994), which articulated three core criteria: (1) scientific or technological advancement, (2) scientific or technological uncertainty, and (3) scientific and technical content. In 1998, Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada synthesized IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) into the landmark Five Questions in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), which formed the basis of the CRA's Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy from 2012 until August 2021.

On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), the CRA archived its 2012 policy and issued the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, restructuring the administrative evaluation into a two-step methodology centred on two foundational requirements—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement. As both the CRA and the Federal Court of Appeal (National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, applying Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88) have confirmed, the "Why and How" guidelines are derived directly from the unchanged text of subsection 248(1) and do not relax the common-law requirement to follow the scientific method established in Northwest Hydraulic.

body.text: Under the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, reviewers evaluate claims through two sequential steps. In Step 1 (Determine Whether SR&ED Exists), the claimant must satisfy both the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement. Under the "Why" Requirement, the work must be conducted to generate or discover conceptual knowledge (such as underlying scientific relationships, theories, or predictive models) rather than merely factual knowledge (such as routine measurements). Technological uncertainty exists when it cannot be determined whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, based on the combined knowledge held within the business and publicly available scientific or technological knowledge accessible to competent professionals in the field. Indicators of technological uncertainty include the inapplicability of established design methods, non-conformance to existing standards, excessive or interlocking variables and constraints, parameters outside normal operating ranges, or system-level integration uncertainties. Workarounds that circumvent the uncertainty using known techniques, or acquiring existing knowledge via training, on-the-job learning, hiring consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary technology, fail the "Why" requirement. Crucially, commercial success or failure is irrelevant: proving through systematic experimentation that a hypothesis is invalid advances technological knowledge and satisfies the "Why" requirement (Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen). Under the "How" Requirement, executing work in an organized manner or following standard engineering protocols is insufficient; the claimant must conduct a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis. This requires four mandatory elements: (i) defining the problem, (ii) formulating a testable hypothesis, (iii) planning and testing the hypothesis through experiment or analysis, and (iv) drawing logical conclusions from the results while retaining contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

In Step 2 (Determine the Extent of Eligible Work), once an eligible core project under paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), or (c) is established, the claimant defines the project boundaries to capture all interrelated experimental cycles and incorporates eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) (engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research) that is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core work, while excluding any commercial or routine activities listed in paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k).
2. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, and Carryforwards
2.1 The Bill C-15 Reform Package (Royal Assent: March 26, 2026)

Following consultations launched in 2024, the Department of Finance released initial proposals in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (and draft legislation on August 15, 2025) that had proposed increasing the enhanced SR&ED expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million. However, in the Federal Budget tabled on November 4, 2025 by the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue, the Government of Canada further increased the enhanced expenditure limit to $6 million. These measures were enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, and apply retroactively to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024).

body.text: 2.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Mechanics: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline annual Expenditure Limit under ITA subsection 127(10.2) is $6,000,000 (prorated by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365 if the taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks). Associated corporations under section 256 must share a single $6,000,000 limit and allocate it via T2 Schedule 49 under subsection 127(10.3). If an associated group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days of a written request by the Minister, the Minister allocates the limit under subsection 127(10.4).

A notable statutory exception applies to the association rules for SR&ED purposes: under the group-control relieving provision, two CCPCs that are associated solely because they are controlled by the same group of persons (without cross-ownership or acting in concert to avoid tax) are deemed not to be associated for calculating the expenditure limit and refundable ITC, provided at least one shareholder of one corporation is not a shareholder of the other and the shareholding was not established to satisfy this exception. Conversely, subsection 256(1.4) treats options, warrants, Simple Agreements for Future Equity (SAFEs), and convertible notes as exercised when determining corporate control.
Method 1: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out (Standard CCPC Method)

Under subsection 127(10.2), a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, reaching nil ($0) at $75,000,000:

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Mathematically, because the $6,000,000 limit phases out across a $60,000,000 capital band ($75,000,000 minus $15,000,000), the expenditure limit shrinks by $0.10 for every $1.00 of prior-year taxable capital in excess of $15,000,000. (Note: An earlier figure of $0.075 per $1.00 referenced in some 2025 commentary reflected the interim $4.5 million expenditure limit proposal divided by the $60 million band prior to the November 4, 2025 budget increase to $6 million).

Taxable capital employed in Canada is determined under Part I.3 of the ITA (sections 181 and 181.2) and ITR section 8601, using non-consolidated GAAP balance sheets. Under section 181.2, taxable capital includes share capital (common and preferred shares), retained earnings, contributed and other surpluses, reserves, and loans, advances, notes payable, bonds, mortgages, and similar indebtedness, minus any GAAP accounting deficit reported on the balance sheet (and minus eligible investment allowances). Whenever a CCPC's prior-year taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000, it must file T2 Schedule 33 (Taxable Capital Employed in Canada – Large Corporations).
Method 2: Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out (ECPCs and Electing CCPCs)

To prevent capital-intensive start-ups—such as biotechnology, clean technology, hardware, and deep-tech firms that raise large equity or debt rounds before generating commercial revenue—from losing access to the 35% refundable credit due to high balance-sheet share capital or debt, Bill C-15 enacted subsections 127(10.31), 127(10.32), 127(10.6), and 127(10.64). Under these provisions, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) must determine their expenditure limit using the gross revenue phase-out formula, whereas CCPCs (either a standalone CCPC under subsection 127(10.31) or an associated group of CCPCs electing together on a prescribed form under subsection 127(10.32)) may elect annually to have their expenditure limit determined under the gross revenue method instead of the taxable capital method.

Under subsection 127(10.6), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on the exact same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 straight-line band ($0.10 reduction per $1.00 over $15 million), but the variable is the corporation's (or consolidated/associated group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years. For standalone corporations, gross revenue is taken from GAAP annual financial statements presented to shareholders; for members of a corporate group preparing consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is measured at the highest level of consolidation with reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales so the group is measured as a single economic entity. Under subsection 127(10.64), if a corporation has fewer than three preceding fiscal years, the average is computed over the available preceding fiscal years, and any short fiscal year under 51 weeks is annualized.
2.3 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) qualifies for the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED ITC up to its annual expenditure limit. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory conditions:

items: Canadian Residency: It must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year.

Public Corporation Status: It must have a class of shares listed on a designated Canadian or foreign stock exchange (such as the TSX, NYSE, or NASDAQ), or have elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation.
Absence of Non-Resident Control: It must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons.

body.text: In addition, a Canadian-resident corporation that is not itself listed on a stock exchange—and therefore is not a CCPC because it is controlled by a public corporation—also qualifies for the enhanced 35% refundable ECPC regime if all or substantially all (90% or more) of the shares of its capital stock are owned by one or more ECPCs. Unlike qualifying CCPCs, however, an ECPC is never eligible for the 40% partial refund on the basic 15% ITC for expenditures exceeding its annual expenditure limit.
2.4 Comprehensive Rate and Refundability Matrix by Claimant Type

The rate at which an SR&ED ITC is earned (35% vs. 15%) and the percentage of unused ITC that is refunded in cash (100%, 40%, or 0%) are governed by ITA subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01). Under subsection 127.1(2), a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" for a taxation year if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation years ending in the preceding calendar year) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. The baseline Qualifying Income Limit is $500,000, and it phases out on a straight-line basis over the same prior-year taxable capital band of $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; previously $10M to $50M). Consequently, a loss-making CCPC with $0 prior-year taxable income remains a "qualifying corporation" as long as its prior-year taxable capital is strictly below $75,000,000; once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000, its Qualifying Income Limit hits zero and it ceases to be a qualifying corporation.

body.text: Special statutory restrictions govern partnerships under ITA paragraphs 96(1)(e.1) and 96(1)(g) and subsections 127(8) to 127(8.5). Because a partnership is not a "person" or "taxpayer" under subsection 248(1), the subsection 37(1) pool must be deducted in full in computing the partnership's net income in the fiscal period incurred; a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 expenditure pool or an ITC pool. Furthermore, under subsection 127(8), a partnership's ITC is always computed at the 15% basic rate—even if all partners are qualifying CCPCs (All Colour Chemicals)—and allocated to active general partners. Under paragraph 127(8)(b), no share of a partnership's SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of the partnership, which includes any limited partner (defined in subsection 96(2.4)) as well as any passive general partner not regularly, continuously, and substantially engaged in the partnership's business activities.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Capital/Lease Restoration
3.1 Election Between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method

Under ITA subsection 37(8) and ITR section 2900, a claimant must choose each taxation year between two mutually exclusive methods for calculating SR&ED expenditures on Form T661 (Lines 160 and 162): the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). Under ITA subsection 37(10) and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, the election is made annually when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is strictly irrevocable for that taxation year once filed. If a claimant does not explicitly elect the Proxy Method on Form T661, the Traditional Method applies by default.

body.text: 3.2 Detailed Eligibility Rules by Expenditure Category
3.2.1 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

Under ITA subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means employment income computed under sections 5 to 8 of the ITA (reported on T4 slips), excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances. Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV)), only salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (meaning hands-on technical work determined by tasks performed rather than job title) may be claimed. Under the All or Substantially All (ASA) Rule (ITR subsection 2900(5)), if an employee directly engaged in SR&ED spends 90% or more of their total working time in the taxation year on eligible SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be claimed.

Several items are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages under ITA section 37 and the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025): the employer's share of payroll-related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or workers' compensation contributions, which are covered by the PPA under the proxy method or claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the traditional method); extended vacation leave or extended sick leave (during which the employee is not directly engaged in SR&ED); stock option benefits under ITA section 7 (legislatively excluded after November 14, 2005, following Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149); unenforceable bonuses (where the employer had no contractual obligation to pay) and non-cash taxable benefits under ITA section 6 (such as company automobiles, housing/board, low-interest loans, or group term life insurance); and retiring allowances.
Strict Statutory Caps for "Specified Employees"

A specified employee is defined in ITA subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer, or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly (including shares owned by non-arm's-length persons such as a spouse, sibling, parent, or child), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of any corporation related to the employer at any time in the year. Specified employees (reported on Line 305 of Form T661) are subject to two layers of statutory caps based on the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan. Under official CRA and Canada Pension Plan parameters, the first earnings ceiling (YMPE) is $71,300 for calendar year 2025 and $74,600 for calendar year 2026 (and was announced on October 28, 2026 to rise to $76,700 for 2027). (Note: While the enhanced CPP regime introduced a second earnings ceiling—the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings [YAMPE] of $81,200 in 2025 and $85,000 in 2026—the SR&ED formulas in the ITA and ITR specifically reference the first ceiling YMPE under Section 18 of the CPP).

The first layer of restriction is the Section 37 Deduction and Direct Wage Cap (ITA Subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1)–(9.5)). Specified employees cannot claim any bonuses or remuneration based on profits (subsection 37(9)). Under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum deductible SR&ED salary or wages for a specified employee (Line 305) is capped at 5 × YMPE, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year in which the individual is employed. For a full 365-day 2025 taxation year (YMPE = $71,300), the 5 × YMPE cap is $356,500; for a full 365-day 2026 taxation year (YMPE = $74,600), the 5 × YMPE cap is $373,000. Under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed unless the associated corporations file an allocation agreement on Form T1174 (supported by a certified directors' resolution) on or before each corporation's SR&ED reporting deadline.

The second layer of restriction is the Proxy Method Salary Base Cap (ITR Subsections 2900(7) to 2900(10), Form T661 Part 5 Boxes 850–860). When computing the Salary Base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), ITR subsection 2900(9) first strips out all taxable benefits, bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and prior-year unpaid wages for all employees. Then, for each specified employee, ITR subsection 2900(7) restricts the includable salary base (Box 860) to the lesser of: (1) the 75% Cap (Boxes 852 × 854 = Box 856), which equals the specified employee's total eligible salary or wages for the year (100% of SR&ED and non-SR&ED base pay, Box 852) multiplied by the actual percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED, capped at a maximum of 75% (Box 854)—meaning that even if a founder or specified employee spends 100% of their time on SR&ED, at most 75% of their salary can enter the PPA salary base; and (2) the 2.5 × YMPE Cap (Box 858), calculated under the statutory formula:
2.5 × A × B ÷ 365, where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year in which the individual is an employee of the claimant.

For a full 365-day 2025 taxation year (YMPE = $71,300), the 2.5 × YMPE cap is $178,250 (generating at 55% a maximum PPA of $98,037.50); for a full 365-day 2026 taxation year (YMPE = $74,600), the 2.5 × YMPE cap is $186,500 (generating at 55% a maximum PPA of $102,575.00). Under ITR subsections 2900(8) and 2900(10), this 2.5 × YMPE limit must be shared across all associated corporations employing that specified employee in taxation years ending in the same calendar year.
Unpaid Remuneration (ITA Subsection 78(4)) and Foreign SR&ED Wages (ITA Subsections 37(1.4)–(1.5))

Under ITA subsection 78(4), any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of that taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year. To preserve the right to claim those wages when paid in a later year, the claimant must identify the unpaid wages on Line 315 of Form T661 by the reporting deadline for the year incurred (subsection 37(11)), and then claim them on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year when actually paid. However, prior-year unpaid wages paid in a subsequent year (Line 310) can never be included in the PPA salary base. Conditional wages payable only if an SR&ED claim is approved by the CRA are contingent liabilities disallowed under ITA paragraph 18(1)(e) (Jaft v. The Queen, 2015 MBCA 77).

Under ITA subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) (Form T661 Line 307), permissible salary or wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada may be included in the Section 37 and Section 127 pools up to the lesser of Amount A and Amount B. Amount A is the total foreign SR&ED wages satisfying all five statutory conditions: (1) performed directly by an employee of the claimant (never a subcontractor), (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred, (3) related to a business of the claimant, (4) an integral part and solely in support of an SR&ED project carried on in Canada, and (5) not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by a foreign country. Amount B is 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salary and wages for work performed in Canada (10% of Line 306).
3.2.2 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Overall Cap vs. Traditional Method Overhead and Cloud Costs

Under ITR subsection 2900(4), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is 55% of the eligible Salary Base (Line 818 × 55% = Line 820). However, ITR subsection 2900(6) imposes an Overall PPA Cap so that the sum of the PPA and other deductions cannot exceed the claimant's total business deductions for the year:
PPA ≤ A − B − C

Where A is total business deductions claimed in computing net income for tax purposes (including cost of goods sold), B is the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed under ITA sections 20 (CCA, interest, bad debts), 24, 26, 30, 32, 37 (SR&ED pool deduction on Schedule 1 Line 411), 66 to 66.8, and 104, and C is expenditures incurred for the use of, or right to use, a building (rent). As a practical benchmark, the Overall PPA Cap will not restrict a claimant's PPA as long as the claimant deducts more than $55 of non-SR&ED ordinary business expenses (excluding Section 20 CCA/interest and building rent) for every $100 of eligible SR&ED salary base.

If a claimant instead elects the Traditional Method, it must itemize actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 and prove under ITA subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and ITR paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b) that each cost satisfies two cumulative tests: (1) the "Directly Related" Test, meaning the expense connects directly to the SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or SR&ED equipment with no intervening step or intermediary; and (2) the "Incremental" Test, meaning the expense would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

Cloud Computing and Software Subscriptions: Under the Proxy Method, third-party cloud computing costs and software or CAD subscriptions are classified as overhead covered by the 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately. Under the Traditional Method, cloud computing and software fees can be claimed on Line 360 only if they satisfy both the directly related and incremental tests (for example, dedicated cloud clusters provisioned specifically to run an experiment and shut down once testing concludes).

Even under the Traditional Method, ITR section 2902 strictly excludes Prescribed Expenditures from qualifying for SR&ED, including: general administration or management of a business (subparagraph 2902(a)(i)); legal or accounting fees, including fees paid to consultants or accountants for preparing SR&ED claims (clause 2902(a)(i)(B)); interest and financing expenses (clause 2902(a)(i)(C)); entertainment expenses (clause 2902(a)(i)(D)); convention and conference expenses (clause 2902(a)(i)(F)); payments for the acquisition of rights in or arising out of SR&ED (ITA subsection 37(4) and ITR paragraph 2902(c)); and charitable donations (ITA subsection 37(5) and ITR paragraph 2902(d)).
3.2.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Prototypes, and Production Runs

Under ITA subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), ITR paragraph 2900(2)(a), and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), a claimant under either the Traditional or Proxy Method may claim 100% of the laid-down cost (invoice cost plus customs, excise duties, freight, storage, and, for internally manufactured inventory, direct labour and production overhead) of tangible, physical raw materials or substances that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is performed or that results from SR&ED. Materials may only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (not when purchased into inventory). Materials Consumed are rendered virtually valueless (having a residual or scrap value of less than 10% of original cost) as a result of the SR&ED testing or experimentation and are not subject to ITC recapture. Materials Transformed are changed or incorporated into another material, prototype, custom product, or commercial asset during SR&ED and retain some value (10% or more of original cost) to the claimant or a third party. If the resulting property incorporating transformed materials is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years, the ITC Recapture Rules under ITA subsections 127(27) to 127(36) apply.

Under the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, Experimental Prototypes—original trial models constructed solely to test a hypothesis during a systematic investigation that have no lasting commercial value (<10% residual value)—qualify in full for direct labour and materials consumed. Pilot Plants—dedicated, non-commercial experimental facilities sized and operated throughout their useful life for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED—qualify for current operating labour and materials under Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) rules. For Custom Products (built for sale) and Commercial Assets (built for internal use), engineering and materials costs are restricted strictly to the specific components undergoing SR&ED (and dependent components forced to be redesigned by the SR&ED), excluding unaffected commercial components. Finally, where experimental development occurs in a production run involving genuine technical risk to the process or product (ED+EP), the direct labour and materials required for the experimental evaluation (excluding excess production) are allowable. Where experimental trials are conducted simultaneously with ongoing commercial production with minimal parameter modifications and no technical risk to product quality (ED+CP), standard commercial production costs are excluded and only incremental SR&ED costs (actual run costs minus verifiable standard commercial production costs) may be claimed.
3.2.4 Arm's-Length Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

Under ITA subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9) (definition of "qualified expenditure", paragraph (g)), when a claimant contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier to perform SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant (Form T661 Line 340), 100% of the current contract expenditure is included in the Section 37 deduction pool and 80% is included in the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. (The 20% statutory reduction is deducted on Line 529 of Form T661). To prevent duplication of ITCs, the contractor must deduct the contract payment received from its own SR&ED expenditures under ITA paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18). Under the Look-Through Rule (ITA subsections 37(14) and 37(15)), the payer must reduce its contract claim by any non-current expenditure incurred by the contractor, and the contractor must notify the payer in writing within 90 days of calendar year-end. Foreign contractor costs for work outside Canada cannot be claimed on Form T661 and earn no ITCs.

For Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts, under ITA subsection 127(9) (paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure"), payments made to a NAL party for performing SR&ED are deductible under Section 37 but do not qualify for ITCs in the hands of the payer, nor is the NAL payment treated as a "contract payment" that reduces the NAL performer's ITC pool. Instead, under ITA subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and the payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures (including its PPA, capped at the contract amount) to the payer. Under ITA subsection 37(13), support work performed by a NAL contractor is deemed to be SR&ED if it would have constituted SR&ED had it been performed directly by the payer. Furthermore, under ITA subsections 127(11.6) to 127(11.8), whenever a claimant acquires goods or services from a NAL supplier for SR&ED, the qualified expenditure is restricted to the NAL supplier's adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost, stripping out all intercompany profit. An anti-avoidance rule in ITA subsection 127(24) denies qualified expenditure status if an arm's-length intermediary is inserted between NAL parties to circumvent these rules.

For Third-Party Payments (Form T661 Line 370 & Form T1263), under ITA subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and 37(1)(a)(ii), payments made to an approved university, college, research institute, or non-profit SR&ED corporation in Canada for SR&ED related to the claimant's business (where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results) are 100% deductible under Section 37 and 80% eligible for ITCs under Section 127, and must be reported on Form T1263.
3.3 Post-December 15, 2024 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, SUE, and Equipment Leases

Under Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), capital property and equipment lease costs are once again eligible for SR&ED tax incentives:

items: SR&ED Capital Expenditures (ASA ≥90% Intent Test — ITA Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) & (B)(III), Line 390): Depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (once available for use under ITA subsections 13(27) and 37(1.2)) qualifies if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant satisfies the Intent Test by intending that the property either be used during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or have ASA (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Eligible assets include laboratory and testing apparatus, prototyping machinery, specialized tools, and compute/GPU infrastructure acquired after December 15, 2024. Under ITA paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e), land, leasehold interests in land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings (other than a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance under ITR section 2903) are strictly excluded. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, filing cabinets, photocopiers, telephones—though computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are not considered GPOEF) is also excluded. Brand-new property qualifies for both the 100% immediate deduction in the Section 37 pool (in lieu of regular Schedule 8 CCA) and the Section 127 ITC (where the 35% enhanced ITC on capital expenditures is 40% refundable). Under ITR paragraph 2902(b), used depreciable property qualifies for the Section 37 income deduction but is excluded from earning Section 127 ITCs, unless refurbished by a vendor so extensively prior to acquisition that it is considered new when acquired.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — ITA Subsection 127(9) & Paragraph 127(11.5)(b), Line 504): Where a claimant acquires brand-new depreciable equipment after December 15, 2024 (excluding GPOEF and excluding Prescribed Depreciable Property [PDP] defined in ITR subsection 2900(11), such as commercial plant commissioning equipment) that does not meet the 90% ASA intent test, it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if it is actually used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. SUE is depreciated under ordinary CCA rules on T2 Schedule 8 (its cost is not added to the Section 37 pool). However, for ITC purposes (under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods), the claimant claims on Line 504 of Form T661 25% (1/4) of the capital cost as First-Term SUE if used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED during the First Period (from acquisition/available-for-use date to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that date), plus an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost as Second-Term SUE (for a cumulative 50% of capital cost) if the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and continues to be used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED during the Second Period (from acquisition date to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that date).

Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024 — ITA Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) & 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)/(VI)): Lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, for equipment (excluding buildings, which are disallowed under ITA subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i)) qualify under both calculation methods. Under the Proxy Method, 100% of the lease cost is allowable if the leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time for SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); 50% of the lease cost is allowable if the equipment (other than GPOEF) is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); and 0% is allowable if used 50% or less, or if the lease is for GPOEF or land. Under the Traditional Method, 100% of the lease cost is allowable as a lease expenditure if used ASA (90% or more) for SR&ED (including GPOEF) (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), whereas if used less than 90% for SR&ED, the actual proportional percentage of SR&ED operating time is claimable as overhead and other expenditures (Line 360) provided it is directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and ITR paragraph 2900(2)(c)).

20-Year ITC Recapture and Deemed CCA Recapture (ITA Subsections 127(27) to 127(36), T2 Schedule 31 Part 24): If any property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned (including transformed materials, custom products/commercial assets, ASA capital equipment, or SUE) is sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years of acquisition, the claimant must add a Recapture Amount directly to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion under ITA subsection 127(27) and subsection 127(36): the lesser of (a) the ITC that can reasonably be considered to have been earned on the property, and (b) the ITC rate originally applied multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (for an arm's-length sale) or the fair market value (for a conversion to commercial use or a non-arm's-length disposition), using 25% of that amount for First-Term SUE and 50% for Second-Term SUE.

body.text: Any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax payable increases the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year under ITA paragraph 37(1)(c.2). Additionally, because Section 37 capital deductions are deemed to be CCA allowed, disposing of Section 37 capital property triggers deemed CCA recapture into income.
4. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, Reviews, and Penalties
4.1 Prescribed Forms and 2026 Reporting Updates

An SR&ED claim is filed as an integral part of the taxpayer's annual income tax return. In May 2026, the CRA released updated versions of its core SR&ED forms to incorporate the Bill C-15 legislative amendments and the Pre-Claim Approval regime.

The core technical and financial form is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026, accompanied by Guide T4088). Part 1 captures general corporate information. Part 2 (Project Data) requires a project-by-project technical narrative detailing the scientific or technological uncertainties, hypotheses formulated, systematic testing and analysis conducted, and advancements achieved. Key 2026 additions to Part 2 include Line 207 (CRDC Field of Research Code), which requires entering the first 5 digits (RDF#####) of the Field of Research (FOR) code from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0; Lines 212 and 214 (Pre-Claim Approval), where claimants tick Line 212 if pre-claim approval was granted for the project and enter the pre-claim approval case number on Line 214; and Lines 262 and 263 (Capital Expenditures Information), which require listing the names of up to the 10 most expensive depreciable SR&ED properties acquired after December 15, 2024, claimed on Line 390 (Line 262) and the percentage of total operating time for each property (Line 263). Part 3 computes current expenditures (Lines 300–380) and post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures (Line 390). Part 4 calculates the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (including Line 502 PPA, Line 504 SUE, Line 529 20% contract/third-party reduction, and Line 570 Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures). Part 5 calculates the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Lines 810–814 for non-specified employees and Boxes 850–860 / Line 816 for specified employees to determine the 55% PPA on Line 820). Part 9 (Lines 935, 970, 975) mandates disclosure of all claim preparer billing arrangements under ITA subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3), and Part 10 contains the authorized signing certification.

Alongside Form T661, corporate claimants must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, updated May 22, 2026) and individual claimants must file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit – Individuals) to claim ITCs, carrybacks/carryforwards, refunds, and Part 24 ITC recapture. Other prescribed forms include Form T1322 (Application for SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval, released April 1, 2026); T2 Schedule 49 (updated May 29, 2026, allocating the $6M expenditure limit among associated CCPCs); Form T1145 (updated May 15, 2026, allocating assistance between NAL parties); Form T1146 (updated May 15, 2026, transferring qualified expenditures under NAL contracts); Form T1174 (allocating specified employee salaries among associated corporations); and Form T1263 (reporting third-party payments).
4.2 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Absolute 18-Month Bar

Under ITA subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (as detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, updated January 28, 2025), a taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

headers: Statutory SR&ED Reporting Deadline (ITA s. 37(11) & s. 127(9)(m))

cells: 6 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year (ITA s. 150(1)(a))
18 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year (6 months + 12 months)
6 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year
6 months after the end of the taxation year (on or before the T2 filing-due date)
17.5 months after the calendar year-end (June 15 of the second following year)
90 days after the end of the trust's taxation year
15 months (90 days + 12 months) after the end of the trust's taxation year
Per Guide T4068 (deemed 6 months after year-end for assistance rules; June 15 for individual partners)
Partners file T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) (with partnership T661 if exempt from T5013) by their respective 18-month or 17.5-month deadline

body.text: Strictness of the 18-Month Deadline: If the SR&ED reporting deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, the claim is on time if received or postmarked on the next business day. Beyond this rule, the 18-month deadline is an absolute statutory bar. Since the legislative amendment of November 17, 2005, ITA subsection 220(2.2) provides no statutory mechanism to extend or waive a missed SR&ED reporting deadline (Datacalc Research, Easyway Cattle, Westsource). If a corporation files its Form T661 on time but fails to file Schedule T2SCH31 until after the 18-month deadline, the corporation may still include the allowable expenditures in its Section 37 deduction pool, but it permanently forfeits all Section 127 ITCs for that taxation year. If Form T661 itself is not filed with the prescribed project and line-item information by the 18-month deadline, both the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 ITC are permanently lost.
4.3 Optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval program to provide businesses with upfront certainty regarding whether proposed or ongoing R&D projects meet the technical eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1) before substantial resources are committed or an income tax return is filed. Claimants complete Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval) and submit it electronically through the CRA's My Business Account portal. The CRA issues a formal technical eligibility determination within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application, and can approve an eligible project for a period of up to three years, subject to the conditions of the program. Because pre-claim approval determines the technical eligibility of the proposed work rather than the final quantum of expenditures, claimants granted pre-claim approval must still file Form T661 (checking Line 212 and entering their pre-claim approval case number on Line 214) and Schedule T2SCH31 with their annual tax return before the 18-month deadline. Pre-approved claims benefit from an accelerated 90-calendar-day processing standard if selected for post-filing verification.
4.4 CRA Service Standards, Technical & Financial Review Process, and Dispute Resolution

When an SR&ED claim is filed with the CRA, it is screened (including through AI-supported risk screening implemented in 2025–2026 to fast-track low-risk claims) and either accepted as filed or referred for a coordinated technical and financial review. The CRA's published service standards (targeted to be met 90% of the time) are 60 calendar days from the receipt of a complete claim for Claims Accepted as Filed, and 180 calendar days from the receipt of a complete claim for Refundable Claims Selected for Review (there is no formal service standard for non-refundable claims selected for review).

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025 and April 20, 2026, replacing The SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants), a review is conducted by two distinct CRA specialists: (1) the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]), who evaluates whether the claimed work meets subsection 248(1) and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report; and (2) the Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]), who verifies the claimed expenditures on Form T661, time-tracking allocations, unpaid amounts, and government assistance adjustments against the taxpayer's books and records (which must be retained for a minimum of six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate under ITA subsection 230(4)(b)).
The review unfolds in three structured stages:

items: Step 1 (The Start of the Review): The reviewer telephones the claimant to announce the review, identify the RTA and FR, specify the projects and issues under examination, and schedule the review meeting, followed by a formal letter and agenda with a 30-day deadline for submitting requested supporting documentation.

Step 2 (The Review Meeting and Requests for Additional Information): The RTA and FR interview the claimant's technical leads and financial staff, conduct a tour of the premises (conducted virtually via video, screen-sharing, and live demonstrations, or on-site on an exceptional basis), and examine contemporaneous evidence (experimental plans, lab notebooks, Git commit histories, sprint retrospectives, CAD iterations, test logs, photographs/videos, physical prototypes/scrap, timesheets, T4 payroll records, and subcontractor agreements/invoices).

Step 3 (The End of the Review and Proposal Package): If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a Proposal Letter detailing financial and ITC adjustments (and any proposed penalties), and working papers. The claimant has 30 days to submit written representations with additional facts or documentary evidence before the final decision and Notice of (Re)Assessment are issued.

body.text: Under the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (updated December 5, 2025), if a disagreement arises before the file is closed, claimants follow a sequential escalation pathway:

items: Step 1 (Reviewer Discussions): Discuss the factual or technical misunderstanding directly with the RTA and/or FR.
Step 2 (Manager Escalation): Escalate unresolved concerns to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Step 3 (Administrative Review — Form RC532): After receiving the Proposal Package and notifying the reviewers within the 30-day window (and before the file is closed), the claimant may submit Form RC532 to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre, which forwards the request within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director. An Administrative Review is not a second technical audit; it evaluates strictly whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation and policies and whether the claimant received due process.

Formal Notice of Objection (ITA Section 165 — Form T400A): Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, a dissatisfied claimant has a strict statutory deadline of 90 days from the date of the notice to file a formal Notice of Objection using Form T400A (Notice of Objection – Income Tax Act) or online via My Business Account to the CRA Appeals Branch. (If missed, an extension application may be made within 1 year under ITA sections 166.1 and 166.2). If the Appeals Branch confirms the reassessment (or fails to respond within 90 days), the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under either the Informal Procedure (where federal tax/credit in dispute is ≤$25,000 per year or loss determination ≤$50,000) or the General Procedure.

items: Claim Preparer Disclosure Penalties (ITA Subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3)): If incomplete, missing, or inaccurate information regarding a claim preparer and their billing arrangement is entered in Part 9 of Form T661, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty. Under subsection 162(5.2), the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable for paying this penalty (unless the preparer exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill under subsection 162(5.3) that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised).

Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (ITA Subsections 163(2), 163(2.1), and 163(3)): Governed by the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, replacing former Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), every person who, knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim is liable to a penalty equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of understated Part I tax and overstated refundable ITC.

body.text: Crucially, under the CRA's "First-Deducted" Ordering Rule and Entire Refund Rule, when a gross negligence penalty applies to a refundable ITC claim, the 50% penalty is levied on the entire overstated refundable ITC, even if part of the overstatement arose from simple error. Under ITA subsection 163(3), the burden of proof rests on the CRA (on a balance of probabilities) to prove knowing misconduct or gross negligence rather than a mere misunderstanding of the Act. Under ITA section 67.6, gross negligence penalties are non-deductible for tax purposes.
5. Comprehensive Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
5.1 Provincial-Federal Stacking and Government Assistance Interaction Rules

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits (or tax-system grants) that stack on top of the federal SR&ED program. Two universal legal rules govern every provincial and territorial R&D claim. First, the claimant must maintain a permanent establishment (defined under ITR section 8201 and provincial tax statutes) in the claiming province or territory and perform the eligible SR&ED within that jurisdiction; provincial credits follow the physical location of the permanent establishment and payroll where the employees work, not the jurisdiction of corporate incorporation. Second, under ITA paragraph 37(1)(d), subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), and 127(18)–(20), and paragraph 12(1)(x), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (whether refundable in cash or non-refundable and added to a carryforward pool, unless formally waived or renounced on time) constitute government assistance for federal tax purposes. Consequently, a provincial credit reduces both the federal Section 37 deduction pool and the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar. Because the federal 55% PPA is a notional amount that is not included in the Section 37 deduction pool, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit (such as Ontario's OITC) that is earned on the PPA does not reduce the Section 37 pool; instead, the PPA-related portion of the provincial credit is included directly in taxable income under ITA paragraph 12(1)(x) on T2 Schedule 1 in the taxation year it is received, while the entire provincial credit reduces the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for federal ITC purposes.
